summary: Oblivious HTTP lets a client send encrypted HTTP requests through a relay to a gateway. The origin server can't link multiple requests to the same client or tell where they came from, and only limited trust is placed in the forwarding nodes. It is useful where a service wants requests without learning who sent them.

plainLanguage.summary: You pass a sealed note to a helper, who hands it to a teacher without knowing what it says. The teacher reads it but never learns who gave it to the helper.

questions: private http requests through a relay
how does ohttp hide client ip address
what is an ohttp relay and gateway
does oblivious http provide forward secrecy
subtitle: Send HTTP requests through a relay so the server sees the request but not who sent it.

tldr.problem: HTTP requests reveal client identity to servers through the source IP address and connection reuse, and client-configured proxies force a bad trade-off between exposing content and paying for a new connection per request.
tldr.mechanism: The client encrypts a binary HTTP request with HPKE to a gateway's public key and POSTs it to a relay. The relay forwards it without being able to read it, and the gateway decrypts it and returns an encrypted response.
tldr.outcome: The gateway never sees the client's IP address and the relay never sees plaintext HTTP content, but the protocol only works with willing relay and gateway operators, costs more than a direct request, and only helps applications that do not carry state between requests.

today: RFC 9458 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2024, and it has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. Its encapsulation can be reused for other content, with encapsulating DNS messages given as an example in the text.

sections.title: Why Hide the Client
sections.content:
HTTP requests give servers more than the request content. The source IP address of the connection reveals identifying information the client has only limited control over, and requests made from one address can be correlated over time to build a profile. Connection reuse improves performance, but it also lets a server link requests that share a connection.

A client-configured HTTP proxy offers only a partial fix. Without TLS the proxy sees the contents. With TLS a new connection is needed for each request so the origin cannot use the connection to correlate requests, which carries significant performance overhead.

Oblivious HTTP encrypts HTTP messages from a client to a gateway and sends them through a trusted relay. The combination means the gateway never sees the client's IP address and the relay never sees plaintext HTTP message content. Connections can still be reused between the client and relay and between the relay and gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask a question, the person you ask can see your face. Oblivious HTTP is like passing your question through a middleman so the answerer sees the question but not your face.

sections.title: The Four Roles and the Flow
sections.content:
Four parties appear in the protocol. The Client originates requests. The Oblivious Relay Resource (the relay) forwards Encapsulated Requests and Responses between clients and a single gateway. The Oblivious Gateway Resource (the gateway) decrypts an Encapsulated Request, forwards it to a Target Resource, then encapsulates the response. The target handles only ordinary HTTP and might not know Oblivious HTTP is in use.

A client must know the gateway's identity, an HPKE public key for it (with a key identifier and the HPKE algorithms), and a relay that will forward to that gateway. Oblivious HTTP uses a one-to-one mapping between a relay and a gateway.

The client builds an HTTP request, encodes it as a binary HTTP message, encapsulates it with HPKE, and POSTs it to the relay. The relay forwards it to the gateway, which removes the HPKE protection and handles the request. The response travels back the same way, encapsulated by the gateway and unwrapped by the client.

The encryption protects the path between the client and the gateway. It does not protect the path between the client and the target, since both gateway and target are logically under the gateway's control.
sections.plainLanguage: You write a note and seal it. A helper carries it to a teacher, who opens it, looks up the answer, seals the reply and sends it back through the helper. The helper only ever holds sealed envelopes.

sections.title: Key Configuration
sections.content:
To encapsulate a request, the client needs the gateway's key configuration, and that configuration MUST be authenticated and integrity protected so that it can be attributed to the gateway. The RFC does not define how clients obtain it, but it does define a format so that different clients can be configured the same way.

A single Key Config holds an 8-bit Key Identifier, a 16-bit HPKE KEM ID, the HPKE public key (Npk * 8 bits), a 16-bit length, and a list of symmetric algorithm pairs. Each pair is a 16-bit KDF identifier and a 16-bit AEAD identifier. The client picks a preferred configuration and a KDF and AEAD combination from the list.

The media type application/ohttp-keys carries a list of key configurations, each prefixed with a 2-byte length. A client that receives such an object with encoding errors MUST discard it, because differences in how clients recover from errors could be used to segregate them.
sections.plainLanguage: The key configuration is like a public mailbox with a slot anyone can drop sealed notes into, but only the teacher has the key to open it. The mailbox label says which kinds of locks it understands.

sections.title: Encapsulating Requests and Responses
sections.content:
Requests use the media type message/ohttp-req. An Encapsulated Request is a header (key identifier as 8 bits, then KEM, KDF and AEAD identifiers as 16 bits each), the encapsulated KEM shared secret (enc), and the HPKE-protected binary HTTP request. The client builds an info string from message/bhttp request, a zero byte and the header, creates a sending context with SetupBaseS(), and seals the request with empty associated data. The gateway reverses this with SetupBaseR() and Open(), returning an error if the key or algorithm combination is unacceptable or decryption fails.

Responses use message/ohttp-res. The gateway keeps its HPKE receiver context. It exports a secret using the string message/bhttp response, generates a random response_nonce of max(Nn, Nk) bytes, and derives an AEAD key and nonce with the KDF, salted with enc concatenated with the nonce. The Encapsulated Response is the nonce followed by the AEAD-protected response. The client derives the same values from its own sending context.

The same encapsulation can be reused for other content by defining a new media type and new constant strings for the HPKE info and exporter context. The RFC gives encapsulating DNS messages (application/dns-message) as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note gets a fresh lock that only the teacher can open. The teacher answers using a lock made from something only the two of you share, so nobody else, not even the helper, can read the reply.

sections.title: How It Uses HTTP
sections.content:
The client sends the relay an ordinary POST whose content is the Encapsulated Request, with a content type header. Extra fields are allowed only if they are independent of the Encapsulated Request and are fields the relay removes before forwarding, such as Connection or Proxy-Authorization. The relay makes the same kind of request to the gateway, copying the content, and MUST NOT add information without the client being aware of the type of information that might be added.

If the gateway gets a response from the target, it returns a single 200 response containing the Encapsulated Response. If it gets none, it can generate an error such as 504 and encapsulate that the same way.

Error handling depends on where the failure happens. Errors from the relay, or from the gateway before it removes protection, go back unprotected as plain 4xx responses. Errors after successful decapsulation, including target errors, MUST be sent in an Encapsulated Response. An unencrypted response to an outdated key configuration might not reach the client, so the gateway MAY use the problem type ohttp-key, and clients may refresh their configuration when they see an unencapsulated error.

Because the AEAD protection cannot be removed until the whole message arrives, progressive processing of responses is not possible. Clients MUST NOT send a 100-continue expectation, and the gateway MUST generate an error if it receives one.
sections.plainLanguage: To everyone along the way it looks like an ordinary parcel being posted. If the post office rejects the parcel, you get a plain note back. If the teacher rejects your question, the rejection comes back sealed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The goal is that a gateway cannot link a request to the client's network and transport identity or to any other request from that client. Requests from client to relay and relay to gateway MUST use HTTPS to give unlinkability against a network observer. The relay cannot be operated by the same entity as the gateway. Placing the gateway and target together does not harm client privacy.

Client duties: clients MUST have a way to authorize a gateway for a target (for example an allowlist), MUST use an authenticated key configuration, and MUST generate a new HPKE context for every request. Request content such as cookies can still let a server correlate requests.

Relay duties: a relay SHOULD NOT forward unknown fields and MUST NOT add identifying information. A relay that rate limits or blocks abusive clients can reveal information to the gateway and shrink the anonymity set. A relay that carries large volumes provides better privacy, and padding and delays can reduce traffic analysis, though delays SHOULD be added only with client awareness.

Replay: a relay can copy and replay Encapsulated Requests, so the server must reject replays or ensure they have no adverse effect. The enc value can serve as a unique identifier, clients SHOULD include a Date header field so the gateway can limit how long it tracks requests, and clients and relays MUST NOT automatically retry a failed request without a positive signal that it was not processed. If the date was rejected, the client may retry once with the gateway's date, using a fresh HPKE context.

Keys: the design provides no forward secrecy during a key configuration's lifetime and no post-compromise security for responses. Regular key rotation limits the damage from a server key compromise.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules make sure the helper cannot peek, nobody reuses a lock, and a copied sealed note cannot trick the teacher into doing the same thing twice. Changing locks now and then limits damage if a key is stolen.

sections.title: Privacy and Client Configurations
sections.content:
Requests should be linkable only by their content, but the choice of client configuration can leak information. A configuration is the relay URI, the gateway key configuration and the gateway URI. Relays and gateways can see when requests use the same configuration, for example by matching the key identifier.

Each active configuration splits the anonymity set of clients, and reducing the number of active configurations to one is infeasible. Client privacy depends on many other clients using the same configuration. Unique configurations that could track individual clients MUST be prevented by the application, and small groupings should also be avoided. The RFC leaves the method for getting configurations out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone in a crowd wears the same uniform, you cannot tell them apart. If you wear a special hat, everyone can spot you, so the system tries to keep everyone dressed alike.

sections.title: Costs and Deployment Limits
sections.content:
Oblivious HTTP has limited applicability. It needs explicit support from a willing relay and gateway, and it is useful only for applications that do not carry state between requests, since it removes linkage only at the transport layer. The RFC names DNS queries and telemetry submission as examples worth the cost, and mentions anonymous surveys, search queries and location-specific content. It calls the protocol simpler and less costly than systems like Prio or Tor, which can give stronger guarantees at higher operational cost.

It costs more than a direct request: each request needs at least two regular HTTP requests, requests grow with extra fields, encryption metadata and AEAD expansion, and key derivation takes computation. Placing relays on the path between clients and servers avoids much extra delay.

Because a relay maps one-to-one to a gateway, it cannot be used as a generic relay for unknown gateways. TLS-intercepting network management might be incompatible with it, and clients configured for interception might choose to disable it.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending a sealed note through a helper takes more steps than just asking out loud, so it is worth it only when the question is private enough.
